Influence without authority

How do you get people you do not manage to move — and how do you know, before the quarter ends, whether they actually will?

Section 1The meeting that did not say no

On Tuesday, 14 October, at 4.10 in the afternoon, Meera Raghunathan left a conference room on the fourth floor of Ojaswi Health Cloud's office in Bengaluru with what she described that evening to her manager as “a good meeting.” Eleven people had attended. Nobody had objected. Three had said the idea was overdue. The head of platform engineering, Devang Rao, had said — and she wrote the words down — “Conceptually, no argument from me.”

Ojaswi Health Cloud sells a clinical and billing workflow suite to mid-sized hospital chains: roughly 340 hospitals, 61,000 beds, and a renewal cycle that turns on how few times a hospital's IT head has to explain an outage to a medical director. Meera had joined eighteen months earlier as a product manager and had inherited a problem the company had accreted rather than designed. Patient communications — appointment reminders, discharge summaries, pharmacy refill nudges, insurance pre-authorisation status — went out through three separate code paths, built by three separate teams at three separate times. Each had its own template store, its own retry logic, its own relationship with the SMS and WhatsApp gateways. In the September quarter, five of the company's fourteen priority-one incidents had originated in one of those three paths.

Meera's proposal was to consolidate them into a single notification service. The engineering estimate was 140 engineer-days. The work sat entirely inside Devang's platform group, which had eight engineers and therefore about 480 engineer-days in the quarter. Meera did not manage Devang. She did not manage any of his engineers. She did not manage the two other product managers whose roadmaps would have to absorb a migration, nor the sales engineer in Chennai who had promised one large chain a custom template feature that the consolidation would break, nor the compliance lead in Pune whose sign-off was required because patient data would move across a new boundary.

Six weeks later, on 25 November, the platform team's quarter-end review showed 140 engineer-days allocated to reliability hardening, 90 to a data-residency migration, and zero to notifications. Nobody had ever said no. The work had simply never been scheduled. That gap — between a room full of agreement and a quarter full of other people's priorities — is the subject of this page, and the single most reliable predictor of whether a product manager's second year is better than their first.

Section 2The idea, stated precisely

Influence without authority is the practice of obtaining a durable allocation of someone else's resources — their engineers' time, their budget, their attention, their public endorsement — when you have no power to reward or punish them, by making the thing you want a better use of those resources from where they are standing than the alternatives they are currently choosing.

Two words in that definition are doing most of the work. Durable excludes the nod in a meeting; you have influence when the allocation survives the next re-planning session that you are not in the room for. From where they are standing excludes the moral case; the question is never whether your project is objectively important but whether it beats the specific things already on their list, as measured by the things they are actually measured on.

The phrase, and the most widely taught treatment of it, comes from Allan Cohen and David Bradford, who published Influence Without Authority in 1989 after a decade of teaching managers in matrixed organisations. The problem they were addressing was structural and new at the time: as firms moved from clean functional hierarchies to matrix and project-based structures through the 1970s and 1980s, a growing population of people found themselves accountable for outcomes that required resources they did not control. Their answer was a model of reciprocity — the near-universal norm that a benefit received creates an obligation to return one — operating through what they called currencies: the specific things a given counterparty values, which are rarely money and are often as mundane as advance notice, reduced on-call load, or visibility with a particular executive.

Cohen and Bradford were building on older ground. In 1959, the social psychologists John French and Bertram Raven had catalogued five bases of social power — legitimate (position), reward, coercive, expert (they believe you know), and referent (they want your regard) — and observed that the first three are conferred by an organisation chart while the last two are earned regardless of it. In 1979 Rosabeth Moss Kanter documented that middle managers with responsibility and no power become risk-averse and territorial, which is a description of what happens to a product manager who never learns this skill. Robert Cialdini's 1984 catalogue of persuasion principles is frequently conflated with this topic and is not the same thing: Cialdini explains how a person's assent is obtained in a moment, Cohen and Bradford explain how an organisation's resources are redirected over a quarter.

The sentence Meera could say in a room without sounding glib: “I am not asking you to believe this matters more than your roadmap — I am asking whether, if it removes five of your fourteen incidents, it is your roadmap.”

Section 3How it actually works

Practitioners describe this work as five steps. Three of them are usually left implicit, and those three are where most attempts fail.

Step one: identify the true decision-maker for the resource, not the owner of the opinion. Meera had spent six weeks influencing the eleven people in the room. Only one of them — Devang — could move 140 engineer-days. The others could block, slow, or complain, which are real powers, but none of them could cause the work to happen. The implicit step here is separating the allocator (one or two people) from the vetoers (several) from the audience (everyone else), and budgeting your effort accordingly. Meera had inverted the budget: broad, thin, and even.

Step two: establish what the counterparty is actually measured on. Not what they care about personally — what their manager will ask them about in January. Devang's committed objective for the quarter was to reduce priority-one incidents from fourteen to six. Everything on his list existed because it served that number or because someone above him had put it there. This is the step people skip because it feels like cynicism. It is not cynicism; it is the difference between offering someone something they value and offering them something you value.

Step three: price the ask in their units. An ask has a cost, and the cost is never denominated in the asker's enthusiasm. 140 engineer-days out of 480 is 29 per cent of a team's quarter. Stating that number out loud, before the counterparty has to compute it, is one of the most trust-generating things a product manager can do, because it demonstrates that you have taken their constraint seriously enough to do their arithmetic for them.

Step four: find the currency, or reframe until the ask pays for itself. There are two moves available. The first is to pay in a currency the counterparty values: you take on the migration coordination, you absorb the customer escalations, you give them the architectural credit in the quarterly review. The second, stronger move is to re-describe the ask so that it advances their own committed objective — at which point you are not trading at all, you are removing a reason for them to say no.

Step five: convert agreement into a costly signal. A yes that costs nothing predicts nothing. The implicit step, and the one Meera missed entirely, is to end every conversation by asking for something small, specific and dated that the counterparty must actually do: a named engineer, a line item in a sprint, a slide in their own planning deck. If they will not pay a small cost now, they will not pay a large one in January.

Section 4A worked example, line by line

On 2 December, Meera restarted. The first thing she did was arithmetic rather than advocacy. Devang's team had 8 engineers and a 60-working-day quarter: 480 engineer-days of capacity, of which his own planning assumed 15 per cent went to unplanned support, leaving 408 allocatable days. Her ask of 140 days was therefore not 29 per cent of his quarter but 34 per cent of everything he could actually commit. She had been understating it.

Then she costed the thing she was offering. Of the fourteen priority-one incidents in the September quarter, five had originated in the three notification paths: two in the retry logic of the pharmacy service, two in template rendering for discharge summaries, one in a gateway failover. Devang's committed target was a reduction from 14 to 6 — a reduction of 8. The consolidation, if it worked, removed 5 of those 8.

Exhibit 1 — The ask, priced in the counterparty's units. December re-plan, Ojaswi Health Cloud platform group.

Line k is the number that matters. Devang's reliability hardening backlog, when Meera asked him to price it the same way, was costing 34 engineer-days per incident removed. Consolidation was cheaper per unit of his own objective than the work he had already scheduled.

That single ratio — 28 days per incident against 34 — changed the conversation from a request into a comparison, and comparisons are how allocators think. Meera was no longer asking Devang to care about notifications. She was showing him that a portion of his own committed target was available at a lower unit price than he was currently paying, and that the invoice happened to have her name on it.

The second pass: change one input

Now suppose the estimate had come back not at 140 days but at 340. The ratio becomes 340 ÷ 5 = 68 days per incident, twice the price of Devang's existing plan, and the argument collapses. This is worth sitting with, because it is the honest edge of the technique: a well-constructed influence case for a badly-priced piece of work will and should lose.

What Meera would do at 340 days is not argue harder. She would decompose. The five incidents did not cost equally: the two retry-logic failures could be removed by putting a single shared retry library behind the pharmacy path, an estimated 45 days. That gives 45 ÷ 2 = 22.5 days per incident — better than anything on Devang's list — and it converts an unprovable 340-day commitment into a provable 45-day one. If the 45 days remove the two incidents, the evidence for the remaining 295 is no longer Meera's confidence; it is the platform team's own data. The general principle: when the price is wrong, do not change the argument, change the size of the ask until the unit economics work, and let the first tranche buy the credibility that funds the second.

Section 5Nuances a learner must acquire

Influence is not persuasion, and the difference is time

Persuasion changes what someone believes inside a conversation. Influence changes what an organisation does across a planning cycle. Almost every failure a new product manager experiences here is a persuasion success mistaken for an influence success: the room agreed, and the agreement had no carrier. The practical consequence is that the meeting is not the unit of work; the re-planning session six weeks later is, and your job in the meeting is only to install something that survives until then.

The ledger is real, but naming it destroys it

Reciprocity genuinely governs lateral organisations — people return favours, and the returns are tracked with surprising accuracy. But the norm operates only as long as it stays unspoken. A product manager who says “I unblocked your release in August, so I need this now” converts a relationship into a transaction and gets one payment instead of an account. Behave as though there is a ledger; never produce it.

What a person values is mostly what their manager measures

Learners are taught to find out what a stakeholder “cares about,” which sends them looking for personality. The higher-yield question is structural: what number does this person report upward, how often, and to whom? Devang's preferences as an engineer were interesting; his commitment to move from 14 incidents to 6 was decisive. When the two conflict, the commitment wins, and a PM who bets on the preference loses.

Authority is not absent — it is simply not yours

There is always someone who can direct the resource. Escalation is therefore a legitimate instrument, not a failure of influence, but it has a specific and narrow correct use: to resolve a genuine conflict of priorities between two people who have both done their arithmetic and still disagree. Used that way, with both parties present and neither surprised, it costs almost nothing. Used as a first move, or as a surprise, it spends the relationship to buy one quarter.

Trust is topic-specific, not general

A product manager may be entirely trusted on customer evidence and not at all on engineering estimates, and the two accounts do not transfer. This explains an otherwise puzzling pattern: the PM whom everyone likes and no one follows. The diagnostic is to ask, for each stakeholder, on what specific question your word would currently be taken without checking — and to notice that the answer is often narrower than you assumed.

Compliance, consent and commitment are three different outcomes

Compliance is doing the minimum described. Consent is not objecting. Commitment is defending the work when you are not there. Most of what passes for influence produces consent, which is indistinguishable from commitment in the room and completely distinguishable in the quarter. The only reliable separator is whether the counterparty has spent something of their own — capacity, reputation, a slot on their own agenda.

Silence is not support

In a matrixed organisation the default answer to any cross-team request is “not this quarter,” and that answer is almost never spoken, because speaking it invites argument. Absence of opposition is therefore the expected observation whether you are winning or losing, and carries close to zero information. Assume you have not been refused only when you can point to something that was scheduled.

Influence cannot tell you whether you are right

This is the hardest and most important limit. The techniques on this page are equally effective in service of a bad decision, and a product manager who becomes good at them before becoming good at judgement becomes a more efficient source of error. The corrective is to hold the same standard of evidence for yourself that you are asking your counterparty to accept: if Meera's five incidents had been three, she should have wanted to lose.

Section 6Where the practice differs

In consumer products, influence is usually exercised over marketing, design and data science, and the dominant currency is evidence — experiment results, cohort data, a video of a user failing a task. Argument loses to a chart that the other person can re-run themselves, because consumer organisations are already instrumented to settle disputes that way.

In B2B and enterprise products, the decisive currency is customer proximity. Sales and customer success control the relationships, and the product manager who can produce a named account, a named economic buyer and a dated renewal risk has a form of standing that no amount of internal reasoning creates. Ojaswi is a B2B company, and it is not an accident that the strongest thing in Meera's hand was an incident count visible to the hospital chains themselves.

In marketplaces and platforms, the structural difficulty is that your counterparties own opposite sides of the same equation — supply growth and demand quality are frequently in direct tension, and both teams are measured on numbers that your proposal moves in opposite directions. Here reframing rarely works, because there is a genuine conflict rather than a misunderstanding, and the honest move is earlier escalation to whoever owns both sides.

Stage changes the texture more than the substance. In an early-stage company of forty people, influence is fast, personal and reputation-dominated: everyone knows what everyone said, currencies are informal, and one badly-handled escalation is remembered for years. In a large company, influence is slow, structural and calendar-dominated: the planning cycle is the only lever that matters, currencies are formalised into headcount and OKRs, and the skill is knowing that a request made three weeks before planning has perhaps ten times the expected value of the same request made three weeks after.

Section 7Common mistakes

Exhibit 2 — Four failure patterns, their external symptoms and the cheapest test that catches each.
PatternWhat an outsider observesThe underlying misunderstandingCheapest diagnostic
Broadcast influence A polished forum presentation; wide agreement; no change in anyone's plan That conviction spreads from a room, rather than being installed one allocator at a time before the room Count how many attendees heard the proposal for the first time in that meeting. If more than two, the meeting was the wrong instrument.
Trading in your own currency The PM keeps repeating the customer impact; the counterparty keeps repeating their capacity That importance is a property of the proposal rather than of the listener's scoreboard Ask the PM to state the counterparty's committed quarterly objective in one sentence. Hesitation is the finding.
Escalation as a first move Cooperation on this project, and slower responses from that team on everything else for two quarters That a directive from above produces commitment, when it produces compliance and a debt Was the counterparty told, by you, before the escalation happened? A no makes the cost certain.
Mistaking consent for commitment “Conceptually, no argument from me” in October; zero allocation in November That agreement in principle and allocation in practice are the same event Name the engineer and the sprint before leaving the room. If neither can be named, nothing has been agreed.

The four patterns are ordered by how flattering they feel. Broadcast influence feels like leadership; trading in your own currency feels like conviction; escalation feels like decisiveness; accepting consent feels like trust. That is precisely why each survives so long inside an individual career: the behaviour is rewarded in the moment and punished only at the quarter boundary, by which time the causal link has faded and the failure is attributed to the other team.

Section 8What good looks like

Handled well, the same decision is almost undramatic. Three weeks before December planning — not after it — Meera spends an hour with the platform team's own incident data and arrives at Devang's desk with his number, not hers. She asks one question: what is your current cost per incident removed? They work it out together: 34 days. She shows 28, and then immediately shows the version she actually wants him to take — the 45-day slice that removes two incidents at 22.5 days each, with the rest deferred until the evidence exists. She offers two things he cannot easily buy elsewhere: her two product-manager peers' agreement to absorb the migration in their own roadmaps, which she has already secured, and her name on the customer communication if it goes badly.

She leaves with a named engineer, a sprint, and a line in Devang's planning deck that he wrote himself. The compliance lead in Pune is briefed the following morning, before the plan is public, and is asked a question rather than sent a document. The sales engineer in Chennai learns about the template change from Meera on a call, six weeks before the customer would have discovered it. None of this is charisma. All of it is arithmetic, sequence and the discipline of asking for something small enough that the answer has to be real.

Section 9What Meera decides

Meera takes the 45-day slice. The full consolidation is what she believes is right and she does not ask for it, because at 140 days she can win the argument and still lose the quarter, whereas at 45 days she can produce evidence that makes the argument unnecessary in March. The reasoning she gives her manager is worth quoting: the constraint is not Devang's willingness, it is that nobody — including her — can currently prove the incident attribution, and a request that requires trust it has not earned is a request that will be deferred politely forever.

What to learn next follows directly. Stakeholder mapping and management is the discipline that tells you which of the eleven people in the October room were allocators and which were audience, and it is the prerequisite this topic assumes. Building trust with teams and Selling the strategy internally are the two halves of making influence cheaper over time: one lowers the price you pay per ask, the other turns a series of individual asks into a shared direction that other people start defending without you. Organisational politics for PMs is where the uncomfortable cases live — what to do when the interests are genuinely opposed and no reframing exists.

  1. Think of a cross-team request you made in the last quarter that was agreed to and never delivered. What, specifically, did the counterparty spend at the moment they agreed — and if the answer is nothing, what small dated cost could you have asked for instead?
  2. For the person whose resources you most depend on, write down the number they report upward and how often. If you cannot write it without checking, what does that tell you about the quality of the last case you made to them?

Influence Without Authority: The Sentinel Decision at Vistaar Pay

A teaching case on rallying people you don't manage around a decision

1. Opening

It was a little past nine in the morning on Thursday, 25 September 2025, and Ananya Krishnan was already on her third cup of filter coffee at Vistaar Pay's office on 100 Feet Road, Indiranagar, Bengaluru. Ananya, Group Product Manager for Checkout Risk, had six working days before Navratri sale traffic began ramping across the platform on 1 October, and eight before the festive peak on Kalinga Mart, Vistaar Pay's largest merchant account. On her screen was a one-page decision memo she had to circulate by Monday: whether, and how, to ship Sentinel v2, a new fraud-scoring model, before the sale window opened. She did not manage the engineers who would build it, the data scientist who had trained it, the salesperson who owned the client relationship it would affect, or the customer-success lead fielding the client's complaints about fraud. Getting Sentinel v2 shipped, shelved, or reshaped depended entirely on people she had no reporting line to, scattered across four cities and three time zones, each with a legitimate claim on the answer.

2. Company background

Vistaar Pay was founded in 2017 by two IIT Bombay classmates who had watched UPI rewire Indian retail and built a checkout and payment-aggregation layer for online merchants: card and UPI processing, fraud screening, and buy-now-pay-later, all behind a single integration. By 2025 the company was a registered payment aggregator under the Reserve Bank of India's PA guidelines, riding NPCI's UPI rails alongside cards and net banking, and competed for merchant business against Razorpay, Cashfree, Pine Labs and PhonePe's merchant gateway arm. It processed checkout for roughly 42,000 online merchants and an annualised gross merchandise value of about ₹38,400 crore, earning revenue on a take rate of under one percent — a business where trust, uptime and low fraud losses were the entire pitch.

Kalinga Mart was Vistaar Pay's marquee account: an India online marketplace for fashion, home and electronics launched in March 2023 by Zahran Retail Group, a Dubai-headquartered retail conglomerate using it as its entry into Indian e-commerce. Kalinga Mart alone ran about ₹3,450 crore of annualised GMV through Vistaar Pay's checkout, some nine percent of the company's total, and Grace Whitfield, Vistaar Pay's Sales Head, was three weeks from closing a three-year renewal worth roughly ₹31 crore in annual processing revenue. Nobody wanted the festive season to go wrong on this account.

3. The situation

Since early August, Vistaar Pay's risk systems had picked up a surge in card-testing attacks on Kalinga Mart's checkout — automated scripts probing stolen card numbers through small transactions, several of them exploiting a promotional flow that let shoppers convert a cash-on-delivery order to prepaid at checkout for a discount. The Reserve Bank's card-tokenisation rules, in forcing merchants to store fewer raw card numbers, had also shifted more fraud attempts toward exactly this kind of testing. Kalinga Mart absorbed the resulting chargebacks directly, and its margins were thinner than the fashion category's average.

Daniel Cho, Vistaar Pay's data science lead in Toronto, had spent ten weeks training Sentinel v2, a machine-learning fraud model using device fingerprinting and behavioural signals rather than static rules. Backtested on August data, it would have prevented most of the card-testing losses — but it also flagged 4.1 percent of genuine transactions for an extra one-time-password step, against roughly 0.6 percent under the existing rules engine. Daniel wanted two more weeks to retrain the model and bring that false-flag rate down before shipping it into a sale season.

Arvind Rao, VP of Engineering, split his Bengaluru and Pune pods between scaling checkout infrastructure for the projected threefold Diwali traffic spike and finishing a buy-now-pay-later launch already promised to another large client. He had not budgeted engineering time for a new fraud model mid-quarter. In Berlin, Lukas Weber, the checkout design lead, worried that a new step-up screen would undo months of work trimming friction out of the payment flow, and that any untested change now would be blamed on his redesign. In Singapore, Mei Lin Tan, who managed the Kalinga Mart relationship day to day, fielded near-daily calls from Rashid Al Naqbi, Zahran Retail Group's VP of Growth in Dubai, who wanted visible action on fraud before signing off on the renewal terms Grace was negotiating. Grace herself, working from New Jersey against Indian and Gulf hours, did not want fraud losses or checkout friction showing up in the numbers Zahran's leadership would review at renewal. Ananya had convening power and the data, but not one of these people reported to her.

4. The people

Arvind Rao — VP Engineering, Bengaluru (with a pod in Pune)
Owns the only engineers who can build and ship Sentinel v2. Wants to protect committed capacity for traffic scaling and the BNPL launch, and is wary of shipping a new risk model without full regression testing during the platform's highest-traffic weeks of the year.
Daniel Cho — Data Science Lead, Toronto
Built Sentinel v2 and believes in it, but does not want his model's first real-world outing to be a rushed, under-tuned version that damages its credibility — or genuine customers' festive shopping.
Grace Whitfield — Sales Head, New Jersey
Owns the Kalinga Mart account and its renewal, worth roughly ₹31 crore a year. Wants fraud losses down and checkout friction invisible, in that order, before she sits across from Rashid Al Naqbi again.
Mei Lin Tan — Customer Success Lead, Singapore
Manages the daily relationship with Kalinga Mart and hears the client's frustration first. Wants a credible, demonstrable fix she can report back to Dubai — soon, and preferably before the sale peaks.

5. Exhibits

Ananya's memo leaned on three pieces of evidence. Exhibit 1 laid out what each option would likely cost in fraud losses and in genuine sales put at risk during the twenty-day festive window from 1 to 20 October, based on the risk team's modelling of last year's comparable period. Exhibit 2 showed why Arvind's resistance was not simply territorial: his two pods' available capacity for the same window was already stretched thin by prior commitments. Exhibit 3 sketched, plainly, why Ananya's job here was persuasion rather than instruction — nobody in the room worked for her.

Exhibit 1 — Projected fraud loss and at-risk genuine sales, 1–20 October 2025 (₹ crore)

A. Full Sentinel v2 rollout0.505.6090

Source: Vistaar Pay risk analytics, modelled on the 2024 festive window at 2025 projected volumes. "At-risk genuine sales" estimates the value of correctly-approved transactions likely abandoned after an added verification step, based on historical step-up abandonment of 22 percent.

The spread in Exhibit 1 was the whole argument in miniature: shipping Sentinel v2 in full cut fraud loss by roughly ₹1.6 crore against the status quo, but put more than five times that in genuine festive sales at risk of being wrongly blocked — precisely the outcome that would alarm Grace and, through her, Rashid. The phased option, applied only to the riskiest slice of traffic — the card-testing signatures and cash-on-delivery-to-prepaid conversions where the fraud actually concentrated — recovered most of the loss reduction at a fraction of the customer friction.

Exhibit 2 — Bengaluru and Pune engineering capacity, 29 Sept–20 Oct 2025 (person-days)

Exhibit 2 explained Arvind's caution without needing to call it obstruction: with only about ten person-days of slack against a full Sentinel v2 build estimated at ninety, Option A was a reallocation that would visibly delay either the infrastructure work or the BNPL launch. The phased build at thirty-five days was still tight, but close enough, with a modest trim elsewhere, to be a request Arvind could plausibly grant without a fight of his own.

Exhibit 3 — Ananya's stakeholder map: no direct reporting line to any of them

As Exhibit 3 made plain, each of the four sat under a different vice-president, in a different office, on a different clock. Ananya's authority extended only to the memo she wrote and the case she could make; every one of the four could simply decline her request.

6. The options

Option A — Push for the full Sentinel v2 rollout by 1 October. This closed the fraud gap fastest and gave Daniel's model its intended debut at scale. Its cost was concrete: ninety engineering days against roughly ten days of real slack, meaning Ananya would have to ask Arvind to delay the infrastructure scaling or the BNPL launch, and ask Grace to accept ₹5.6 crore of at-risk sales on the account she was about to renew — the two people least likely to say yes to a favour neither owed her.

Option B — Negotiate a phased rollout on the highest-risk segment. Restricting Sentinel v2 to the patterns driving most of the fraud — cash-on-delivery-to-prepaid conversions and known card-testing signatures — cut the engineering ask to thirty-five days, close enough to Arvind's slack to be negotiable, and cut customer-facing friction to about ₹1 crore of at-risk sales, defensible to Rashid. Its cost was that fraud outside the targeted segment continued unchecked, and Daniel's model launched narrower than he had designed it for.

Option C — Delay the model until after Diwali and hold the existing rules engine. This asked almost nothing of anyone and let Daniel finish tuning properly. Its cost fell entirely on the festive window: an estimated ₹2.1 crore in fraud losses Kalinga Mart would absorb during its highest-revenue weeks, precisely when Rashid was watching closest and Grace was mid-renewal.

7. Questions for discussion

  1. What does each of the four stakeholders actually need to say yes — not what they say they want, but what would let them agree without losing standing with their own boss?
  2. Why does Exhibit 2 matter as much as Exhibit 1 to Ananya's case? What does it tell her about which ask is realistic this week and which is not?
  3. If Ananya cannot compel any of the four, what can she trade, sequence, or reframe to build a coalition rather than ask for a favour from each of them separately?
  4. Which option would you choose, and whom would you persuade first — and in what order would you approach the rest?

8. A note for the learner

This case is a stakeholder map with the reporting lines removed. Ananya's problem is not technical — the risk team already knows which model reduces fraud and by how much. Her problem is that four people with four different bosses, four different incentives, and four different time zones each hold a piece of the decision, and none of them work for her. Influence without authority is stakeholder management stripped of the shortcut a manager has: instead of an instruction, Ananya has only a case good enough that each stakeholder chooses, in their own interest, to say yes.

A well-reasoned answer treats Exhibit 2 as decisive before Exhibit 1: an ask that exceeds real capacity fails regardless of how compelling the fraud numbers are, so the first move is sizing the request to what Arvind can actually grant without a fight of his own. Option A's underlying analysis is sound but its execution ignores this — asking for ninety days against ten days of slack, and ₹5.6 crore of at-risk sales on an account mid-renewal, invites two separate refusals from two people Ananya cannot outrank. Option C avoids conflict entirely but simply defers the cost to the exact weeks when it is most visible to the client and most damaging to Grace's renewal conversation, which is not a resolution, only a postponement dressed as prudence.

The defensible path is Option B, built and sold as a coalition rather than a directive. Ananya takes Exhibit 2 to Arvind first, framing the ask as thirty-five days on the highest-value fraud segment rather than a full rebuild — small enough to grant, specific enough to plan around, and something he can defend to his own leadership as protecting the BNPL and infrastructure commitments he already owns. She takes the narrowed false-decline number to Grace next, not as a risk to accept but as the evidence Grace can carry into the renewal conversation herself, turning Mei Lin's daily fire-fighting with Rashid into a story of decisive action. She gives Daniel a real say in the segment definition, so the model he ships is one he can stand behind even if it launches narrower than planned, and she keeps Lukas informed early enough that the step-up screen lands as a small, telegraphed change rather than a surprise he has to defend. None of the four gets everything they asked for; each gets enough of what they need to say yes, and the coalition, not the org chart, is what ships Sentinel v2 in time for Diwali.

Rain Over Old Airport Road: The Dhaara Migration at Nimantran Cloud

A case on moving an organisation you do not manage

1. Sunday night

At 11.20 on the night of Sunday, 4 October 2026, Kaushik Iyer was the only person on the fourth floor of Nimantran Cloud's building on Old Airport Road, Bengaluru, and the rain outside was loud enough that he had given up on calls. In front of him was a single sheet, formatted to the template the Portfolio Council insisted on: problem, recommendation, cost, risks, owner. Nine hours from now he would table it. Every field was filled except the last two.

Kaushik was Principal Product Manager for Platform Foundations. He had been at Nimantran for four years, he was the person most often described in performance calibrations as "the one who actually knows how the system works," and he had, by design, nobody reporting to him. The engineers who would carry out what his memo recommended sat in two pods in Bengaluru and one in Pune, under a Senior Vice President who had not returned his last message. The data scientist whose numbers underpinned the case worked in Toronto. The designer who could make or break the customer experience was in Berlin. The two people who would have to explain the decision to paying customers sat in Singapore and New Jersey, and the customer who mattered most to the quarter was in Dubai.

The recommendation he had planned to make for three weeks was clean: announce, at the company's user conference in Goa on 15 October, that the legacy Chithi Journeys builder would reach end of support on 31 March 2027. On Friday evening, at 7.40, a contracts analyst had sent him a scanned page of a master services agreement he had never been shown. Kaushik had read it four times since. He had not yet told anyone that he had read it.

2. How Nimantran came to have two engines

Nimantran Cloud was founded in Bengaluru in 2016 by three engineers who had watched Indian consumer brands discover, more or less simultaneously, that they could reach customers on a phone for a fraction of what television cost. The product was a customer-engagement platform: it ingested events from a brand's app and website, segmented users, and orchestrated campaigns across SMS, push notifications, email, and later WhatsApp and RCS. By FY26 it ran ₹412 crore of annual recurring revenue across roughly 2,840 paying accounts, about 61 per cent of it from India and the rest from South-East Asia, the Gulf and a small but expensive North American book.

The decision that shaped everything Kaushik now faced had been made four years earlier. In September 2022, Nimantran had acquired Chithi Labs, a forty-six-person company in Pune, for ₹96 crore. Chithi's product was a visual journey builder — a drag-and-drop canvas on which a marketer could assemble a multi-step campaign without writing code — and the acquisition memo argued, persuasively, that building it in-house would take fourteen months the company did not have while MoEngage and CleverTap were winning deals on exactly that feature. The board approved it in a week.

What the diligence had not priced was the shape of the thing underneath. Chithi's engine was a single-tenant architecture from an earlier era of the web, with per-customer configuration held in database rows rather than code, and an escape hatch that let implementation consultants drop arbitrary scripts into a journey step. Customers loved the escape hatch. By 2026 there were roughly 4,100 customer-built journeys in production, of which about 1,300 contained at least one custom script, and a long tail of accounts whose entire lifecycle marketing sat on logic no one at Nimantran had written or documented.

In January 2024 the board approved Dhaara: a single event-driven orchestration engine, multi-tenant, with a declarative journey model and a real-time decisioning layer, budgeted at ₹58 crore over eight quarters. The plan assumed an automated converter would move the great majority of existing journeys across, and that the Pune pod would shrink as Chithi wound down.

3. The market Nimantran sells into

The Indian engagement-software market in 2026 was crowded and, for the first time, price-conscious. MoEngage, CleverTap, Netcore Cloud and WebEngage competed for the same mid-market Indian brands; Braze and Salesforce's marketing stack sat above them in enterprise deals, particularly in the Gulf and North America. Differentiation had migrated from features to two things: channel economics and compliance.

Channel economics had turned sharply. When Meta moved the WhatsApp Business Platform to per-message pricing, a category of campaign that Indian brands had treated as nearly free became a line item finance departments reviewed, and brands began asking their vendors to send fewer messages and prove the ones they sent worked. RCS, carried on Jio and Airtel networks, was growing fast enough that every vendor had to support it and none could yet monetise it.

Compliance had turned sharper still. TRAI's commercial-communications regime required DLT registration of SMS headers and templates, and enforcement had tightened. The Digital Personal Data Protection Act and the rules under it imposed obligations a campaign platform could not push onto its customers: verifiable consent, purpose limitation, and the ability to show, for any message sent to any data principal, the consent under which it went. Neither Chithi Journeys nor, as it happened, Dhaara had a consent ledger that would satisfy a serious auditor. A ledger had sat on the Dhaara roadmap for three quarters and had been deferred three times.

Nimantran's exposure was not domestic alone. Its largest single account, Barzan Retail Holding of Dubai, ran loyalty and lifecycle campaigns for eleven brands across the UAE, Saudi Arabia and Qatar, and its campaign calendar peaked during Ramadan rather than Diwali, which meant that Nimantran's Indian festive freeze and its largest customer's planning cycle were permanently out of phase.

4. What happened, and what has since proved wrong

The Dhaara programme had not failed. It had done something more awkward: it had produced a sequence of results that each looked like success at the time and each turned out, later, to have been measured on the wrong population.

In November 2025 the migration converter shipped, reporting a 78 per cent automatic conversion rate that was repeated in the January board pack. In April 2026 an analyst reran it against a random sample of live customer journeys — rather than the internal demo library it had originally been benchmarked on — and measured 31 per cent for accounts containing custom scripts, 74 per cent for those without. Nobody had lied. The original benchmark had been run on what was available.

In March 2026 the first sixty-one "lighthouse" accounts were migrated and the programme reported a satisfaction score of 4.4 out of 5. In August, Meera Anand's team in Singapore, preparing a renewal forecast, noticed that thirty-eight of those sixty-one accounts had fewer than five journeys each, that nine had quietly asked to be moved back to Chithi, and that the satisfaction survey had been sent only to accounts that completed migration.

In June, after the WhatsApp pricing change, finance's cost-to-serve model showed Chithi accounts as more expensive per thousand messages than Dhaara accounts, which Kaushik had used in every conversation since. In September he learned that cloud cost was allocated across engines by team headcount rather than by usage, and the Pune pod had been cut from forty-nine to thirty-four people in January.

In August, Naveen Kuruvilla circulated a study showing that Dhaara's decisioning layer lifted conversion by 18.2 per cent against Chithi's rules-based sends, across eleven accounts. In late September, reviewing the study for the board pack, Kaushik found that the holdout group had been broken for three weeks in July by a release that routed holdout users into the treatment path, and that only three of the eleven accounts had clean data throughout.

Then there was Friday. The scanned page was Schedule C of the Barzan master services agreement, signed in February 2024 to win the account against a global incumbent. Clause 9.3 committed Nimantran to "continued availability and support of the Chithi Journeys interface and its exported artefacts" through 31 March 2028, with service credits of up to ₹7 crore for material breach. Gregory Alvares had signed it. Nobody had told the Dhaara programme, and the clause did not appear in the contract summary in the CRM.

7. Voices

8. The options as Kaushik sees them

By Sunday night the memo carried three options, and Kaushik was uneasily aware that he had written all three himself, in a form that suited a one-page template.

Option one: announce the date. End of support for Chithi Journeys on 31 March 2027, declared from the stage in Goa on 15 October. The virtue is that a public date is the only forcing function available to somebody with no authority: it converts Kaushik's request into everyone else's deadline. The cost is that the date is not his to promise. It contradicts Schedule C, it lands inside Meera's renewal cycle, and it commits engineering capacity that Exhibit 3 suggests does not exist unless an unwritten integrator contract is signed and funded within weeks.

Option two: dual-run and migrate on renewal. No announced end date; accounts move when their contract comes up, with incentives. This is the option nobody can object to, which is precisely what worries him. It leaves two engines, two on-call rotations and two compliance surfaces, it makes Sudha's reliability numbers harder rather than easier, and it defers the consent ledger indefinitely because the ledger has to be built twice or built in a shared layer that neither pod owns.

Option three: segment and sequence. Migrate the 240 largest accounts by March, price a Chithi surcharge into mid-market renewals, leave the tail where it is. It survives contact with Exhibits 1 and 3. It also requires the most from the most people — Parth's script inventory, Naveen's schema contract, Ilse's consent design, Meera's renewal conversations — which is to say it requires the coalition he does not have.

What nagged at him was that all three options were about the engine and the date, and the three loudest disagreements of the fortnight had been about neither. Ilse's question cut across every option. Parth's inventory would move Exhibit 3 more than any architectural choice would. And Schedule C raised a question the template had no field for: whether an announced date was a decision at all, or merely a claim Barzan's lawyers could price.

There was a fourth possibility he had not written down, because writing it down felt like failure: that the memo should not recommend an engine decision, but should say that Nimantran had no single owner for this migration, and ask the Council to make one. The person best placed to own it was Sudha. If Kaushik proposed that, he would be handing away the programme he had carried for two years, to the person most inclined to postpone it — and he would be doing so in the fortnight before Farah's board conversation.

9. The deadline and the hard constraints

The Portfolio Council met at 9.30 on Monday, 5 October. The user conference in Goa opened on 15 October, and the keynote script locked on the 10th. Engineering entered a change freeze from 20 October to 20 November, across Diwali on 8 November, and FY27 planning locked on 30 November, meaning that anything not funded by then waited until April.

The money was fixed: ₹11 crore remained of Dhaara's ₹58 crore, and a hiring freeze had been in force since June, so any additional capacity had to come from a systems integrator paid out of that ₹11 crore or from another team's headcount. Pune had thirty-four engineers, four of whom held the only working knowledge of the custom-script layer. The Barzan contract ran to 31 March 2028 with ₹7 crore of service credits at stake, and Barzan represented ₹46 crore of ARR, a little over eleven per cent of the company. The DPDP obligations had no negotiable date and applied to both engines equally. Sudha's availability commitment carried customer credits of its own. And Farah, who had said the decision was Kaushik's to drive, would be in the room on Monday.

10. Questions for discussion

  1. Whose agreement does Kaushik actually require by Monday morning, whose by 15 October, and whose not at all? What changes if he is wrong about any of these?
  2. Exhibits 1, 3, 4 and 5 disagree with one another in ways their footnotes explain and their headline numbers hide. Which exhibit would you put in front of the Council, and what does your choice do to the trust you will need in January?
  3. Each of the seven stakeholders is withholding something. For each, what would have to be true for them to say the unsaid thing out loud — and what is Kaushik's part in making that safe?
  4. Parth's incentives point one way and his information points the other. Is there a move available to Kaushik that does not require Parth to volunteer for the elimination of his own team's charter?
  5. Kaushik has framed the decision as engine and date. Argue the case that the real decision is ownership, or consent architecture, or the Barzan contract — and say what the cost is of reframing it on Monday rather than a month ago.
  6. What should Kaushik put in the recommendation and owner fields before 9.30 tomorrow, and if the board asks him in November why the migration is where it is, what should he say — knowing that Sudha, Gregory and Farah will be in that room too?

Monday, 12.40 a.m.

The rain had thinned. Kaushik had two drafts open. One recommended the 31 March date and named Sudha as owner, which she had not agreed to. The other recommended segmentation and named himself, which the Council would read as the programme continuing exactly as it had for two years.

On his phone there was an unsent message to Parth, written at half past ten and reread since: Can we talk before the Council? Not about the date. About what is actually in those scripts. Below it, a message from Meera timestamped 12.14 a.m. Singapore time, asking again for the sentence she was supposed to say to Thaali Mart on Tuesday. And in a separate window, the scanned page of Schedule C, which four people in the company had now read and none had mentioned in any meeting.

He could raise the clause on Monday, which would make Gregory an opponent for a year and might make the Goa announcement impossible for reasons nobody could argue with. He could hold it, and let the Council decide on facts he knew to be incomplete. He could send the message to Parth and arrive at 9.30 with either a collaborator or a leak.

At 12.40 he saved both drafts, named neither, and put the laptop down on the table beside the cold coffee. The Council was in under nine hours, and he still did not know which of the people in Exhibit 6 he was going to call first.

Influence without authority

Rallying people you do not manage — the mechanics, the arithmetic, the seams where it breaks, and the disagreements the field has not settled.

Section 1Two decisions, one structure

On 3 February, Nandita Iyer circulated a two-page memo inside Shreyan Commerce Cloud proposing that the marketplace begin deactivating sellers who miss a 48-hour dispatch commitment three times in a rolling 30-day window. Shreyan, headquartered in Gurugram, connects about 48,000 small apparel sellers — the majority in Surat, Tiruppur and Ludhiana — to roughly 3.1 million monthly buyers. Monthly gross merchandise value is ₹186 crore across 7.4 lakh orders, an average order value of ₹2,514. Nandita is a group product manager for the buyer experience. She controls no sellers, no category teams, no field operations, and no part of the seller-growth organisation whose director, Harsh Vora, carries a committed quarterly target of 6,200 net new active sellers. Her proposal would deactivate 3,100 of them.

Nine hundred and fifty kilometres south, on 6 February, Arvind Menon was working against a harder deadline. Ojasvin Instruments makes connected haematology analysers for pathology laboratories; 2,900 units are installed across 640 labs, generating ₹6.2 lakh per instrument per year in reagents and service contracts. Arvind wants over-the-air reagent-calibration updates, which would remove most of the field-engineer visits that currently keep instruments correctly calibrated. The change requires four things he cannot authorise: a firmware slot from Sunita Kelkar's embedded team, a board revision with additional flash memory from Girish Pai in operations, a re-submission to the Central Drugs Standard Control Organisation prepared by Farhan Qureshi's regulatory group, and the acquiescence of Meenal Deshpande, whose field-service organisation bills ₹4,800 per calibration visit and would lose about 7,200 visits a year. The manufacturing lot freezes on 9 February. After that the next opportunity is August.

The two situations look unrelated — a two-sided consumer marketplace and a regulated hardware-plus-software business — and they share the only structural feature that matters here. In both, the person accountable for an outcome must obtain resources from people whose own scoreboards the outcome does not improve, and in at least one case actively damages. This page is about what is actually known, actually contested, and actually measurable about doing that well.

Section 2The idea and the schools that disagree about it

Influence without authority is the practice of obtaining a durable reallocation of resources you do not control, by changing either the counterparty's payoff from the reallocation or the information on which they compute it. The definition is deliberately narrow in two ways. It excludes momentary assent, because assent that does not survive the next planning cycle is not a reallocation. And it names two, and only two, levers: payoff and information. Everything in the practitioner's repertoire — trading favours, building trust, running experiments, escalating, redesigning a metric — changes one of those two.

The canonical text is Allan Cohen and David Bradford's Influence Without Authority (1989), written for managers in the matrix organisations that had spread through American industry after Jay Galbraith's work on lateral coordination in the 1970s. Their model rests on the norm of reciprocity and on currencies of exchange: the things a particular counterparty values, which are usually not money — advance warning, reduced on-call burden, headcount, a named mention in a review, protection from a customer escalation. Behind them stands John French and Bertram Raven's 1959 taxonomy of power (legitimate, reward, coercive, expert, referent), whose value is the observation that only the first three come from the organisation chart. Alongside them, from a different tradition, Jeffrey Pfeffer's Managing with Power (1992) argues that individual technique is second-order to structural position, and Rosabeth Moss Kanter's 1979 field work established that responsibility without power produces defensiveness rather than ingenuity.

These are not variations on one idea. They are four positions that give different advice in the same situation, and a practitioner who cannot state the difference will apply the wrong one.

A practitioner's implicit school is usually visible in their first move when blocked. The exchange school offers something; the evidentialist runs a study; the structuralist goes to change the forum or the metric; the relationalist goes to lunch.

The disagreement is real and it is not resolvable by synthesis, because the schools make different predictions about the same case. Confronted with Harsh Vora, whose target is damaged by Nandita's proposal, the exchange school looks for a currency large enough to compensate 3,100 seller deactivations — and there is none, since nothing Nandita possesses converts into net new active sellers. The evidentialist says the target itself is the defect: counting sellers rather than sellers who can fulfil is a measurement error, and the argument should be made to whoever owns that definition. The structuralist agrees on the remedy but for a different reason — not that the metric is wrong but that Nandita will lose any contest conducted inside a forum Harsh's function controls. The relationalist observes that Nandita and Harsh have interacted four times in two years and that this is the actual root cause, four quarters too late to fix.

Section 3Mechanics in depth, with the arithmetic

Expert practitioners do something structurally different from novices at the very first step: they compute the counterparty's decision rather than construct their own argument. A resource owner facing more demand than capacity is running an implicit ranking by value per unit of capacity, where value is measured in whatever they are accountable for. Your request succeeds if and only if its value per unit exceeds that of the marginal item — the last thing that currently fits. This is the formal core of the subject, and it is why enthusiasm is irrelevant: enthusiasm does not change a ratio.

Take Arvind's firmware ask. Sunita Kelkar's embedded team has six engineers and a 58-working-day window before the lot freeze, of which she commits 80 per cent, giving 269 allocatable engineer-days. Her accountable measure for the year is field-reported firmware defects per thousand instrument-months, currently 3.4, targeted at 2.0. Arvind's OTA work is estimated at 96 engineer-days — 35.7 per cent of everything she can commit — and, as originally framed, contributes nothing to defect density.

The reframing is not rhetoric; it is an arithmetic claim that can be checked. Ojasvin's embedded team shipped 11 firmware defect fixes last year. Each reached the installed base through the field-service visit cycle, which takes a median of 14 weeks to touch 90 per cent of instruments. Defect-months accumulate during that window. At 2,900 instruments and a 14-week tail, each fix leaves roughly 2,900 × 3.2 months × 0.5 = 4,640 instrument-months of residual exposure; with OTA the tail falls to about four days, near zero. Eleven fixes a year at 4,640 instrument-months each is 51,040 instrument-months of avoided exposure, against an annual denominator of 34,800 instrument-months — which is to say the rollout tail, not the defect rate, is the dominant term in Sunita's own metric. Arvind did not discover this by thinking about influence. He discovered it by reading her dashboard.

Three second-order effects follow, and expert practitioners plan for them explicitly.

First, a successful reframe transfers ownership, and ownership transfers credit. Once OTA is the fastest route to Sunita's defect target, it becomes her project as much as Arvind's, which is exactly what he wants for delivery and exactly what he must not contest in the review. Practitioners who reframe successfully and then reclaim authorship in public find the reframe does not work a second time.

Second, every reallocation displaces something, and the displaced item has an owner. Arvind's 96 days push “UI polish” and “refactor” out of the window. Somebody asked for those. The novice treats the counterparty's yes as the end of the campaign; the expert asks who else was in that queue and pre-empts the resentment, often by telling the displaced party first.

Third, the ask changes the counterparty's risk profile, not only their workload. Over-the-air firmware update on a regulated diagnostic instrument means that a bad push can brick 2,900 machines in laboratories that run patient samples. Sunita's exposure is not 96 days; it is 96 days plus a class of failure she did not previously own. Any offer that does not address that — staged rollout, signed images, a rollback path, Arvind's name on the incident review — is under-priced, and experienced engineers can smell an under-priced ask immediately.

Coalition arithmetic and the value of the pre-wire

Where several parties can each independently block, the probability of clearing them all is the product of the individual probabilities, and the product punishes breadth savagely. Arvind needs four yeses. If, walking into a group forum cold, each is 85 per cent likely, the joint probability is 0.854 = 0.52. Nandita, by contrast, needs six: seller growth, category, buyer support, finance, legal and the marketplace's risk committee. At the same 85 per cent per party, her joint probability is 0.856 = 0.38.

Two implications are not obvious. The first is that reducing the number of approvers is usually worth more than improving the pitch: Nandita can move from six parties to four by scoping the pilot to two categories, which removes finance and the risk committee entirely, and 0.854 = 0.52 beats a heavily-worked 0.906 = 0.53 at a fraction of the effort. The second is that the pre-wire's value comes not from advance agreement but from advance objection. A counterparty who raises a concern privately is cheap to satisfy; the same concern raised publicly commits them to a position they must then defend.

Section 4When the idea applies, and when it misleads

The conditions under which lateral influence works can be stated as testable claims rather than aphorisms. Four matter.

Claim one: there exists a framing under which the proposal improves the counterparty's own measured outcome. For Arvind and Sunita, true — the rollout-tail arithmetic establishes it. For Nandita and Harsh, demonstrably false: no framing converts 3,100 deactivations into net new active sellers, because the metric counts the thing she proposes to destroy. When this claim is false, persisting with persuasion is not merely ineffective, it is actively misleading, because each polite deferral is read as progress.

Claim two: the counterparty controls the resource in question. For Arvind and Girish Pai, this is only partly true. Girish owns the manufacturing schedule but the flash-memory change requires a component qualification that a contract manufacturer owns, and that party has no relationship with Ojasvin's product organisation at all. Influence exercised on a proxy who cannot deliver is the most common source of confident failure.

Claim three: the time available exceeds the time required for the counterparty's own commitment process. Sunita re-plans fortnightly; 6 February leaves one cycle before the freeze. Farhan's regulatory submission takes eleven weeks regardless of enthusiasm. Where the required change is slower than the window, influence is the wrong tool and the right question is what smaller thing preserves the option.

Claim four: the relationship will persist long enough for reciprocity to operate. Reciprocity requires a repeated game. In a reorganisation, an outsourced function, or a contractor relationship ending in six weeks, the mechanism simply is not running, and practitioners who rely on it are surprised to find their credit worthless.

The situation where the whole framework is most actively misleading is the one Nandita occupies: a genuine conflict of interest between two correctly-behaving managers, created by a metric definition. Treating it as an influence problem produces months of increasingly sophisticated persuasion aimed at a person who is doing his job correctly. The structural school's advice — go and change the definition, which requires someone who owns both sides — is faster, more honest and more uncomfortable, which is why it is usually taken last.

Section 5Hard edge cases and the organisational seams

Multi-product platform queues. When one platform team serves five product lines, the marginal-item calculation acquires a second term: fairness. Platform leaders manage a portfolio of relationships and will decline a request that wins on unit value if accepting it would give one product line three consecutive quarters of allocation. The tell is a counterparty who agrees with your arithmetic and declines anyway. Mature organisations handle this by pre-committing capacity shares in the annual plan — Ojasvin allocates the embedded team 60 per cent roadmap, 25 per cent platform debt, 15 per cent unplanned — which converts an argument about priority into an argument about which bucket an item belongs to, a far more tractable dispute.

Two-sided markets. Shreyan's case generalises: in marketplaces the supply and demand organisations are measured on numbers that a quality intervention moves in opposite directions, by construction. There is no currency trade available because the disagreement is not a misunderstanding. What mature marketplaces actually do — as distinct from what they describe in their operating principles — is maintain a small number of “both-sides” metrics owned above both functions, and route exactly this class of decision to them. Where those do not exist, the decision is settled by whichever side has the more senior leader, and everyone involved knows it.

Regulated products. Regulatory affairs is the one counterparty for whom “no” carries no personal cost and “yes” carries career risk, which makes the payoff asymmetry extreme. Farhan Qureshi will not be blamed for a delayed CDSCO submission; he will be blamed for an unsuccessful one. The only effective currency is reduced ambiguity: a written change-classification rationale, a precedent from a comparable device, a pre-submission meeting. Offering speed to a regulatory lead is offering them a currency they are penalised for accepting.

Hardware plus software. The seam is that software has a re-planning cycle of two weeks and hardware has one of six months. A software product manager who arrives with a well-constructed case three weeks after the lot freeze has made an irreversible error that no amount of skill recovers. Practitioners in these businesses keep a standing “option list” — cheap hardware provisions such as extra flash, an unused connector, a spare sensor header — argued for a year before the software case exists, precisely because the influence conversation must happen before the evidence does. Arvind's real failure, if he misses 9 February, dates to the previous August.

AI-native products. When model behaviour is owned by a central research or applied-AI team, the product manager cannot specify the outcome in the usual way: the counterparty cannot promise a behaviour, only an attempt. The currency that works is evaluation sets. A product manager who arrives with 400 labelled examples of the failure mode, a scoring rubric and a baseline measurement has given the model team the thing they are scarcest in — a defensible definition of done — and has converted an untestable request into a queue item that competes on the same footing as everything else. A product manager who arrives with adjectives has not.

Section 6Nine nuances that separate the expert

1. The scoreboard beats the sentiment

Competent practitioners learn what a stakeholder cares about; experts learn what they report upward, in what units and on what date. The tell is a counterparty who is visibly enthusiastic in conversation and structurally absent from delivery. The obvious reading — they were being polite — is usually wrong. They meant it. Their enthusiasm simply has no channel through which to become capacity, and it is the practitioner's job, not theirs, to find one.

2. Consent, compliance and commitment produce identical meetings

Compliance delivers the literal scope. Consent declines to object. Commitment defends the work in rooms you are not in. All three sound the same on the day. The expert's tell is the direction of the questions: a committed counterparty asks about edge cases, sequencing and what happens if it works, because they are already inside the problem. A consenting one asks about scope boundaries and exit conditions, because they are managing exposure.

3. Trust is domain-indexed and does not transfer

A product manager can be fully trusted on customer evidence and not at all on estimates. The tell is a counterparty who accepts your data and re-derives your conclusion. The obvious reading is disrespect; the correct one is that you have an account in one domain and none in the other, and the remedy is to make a small, checkable, dated prediction in the deficient domain and be visibly right about it.

4. The reciprocity account has a half-life

Favours depreciate, and faster than people expect — practitioners who track it put the half-life at roughly one planning cycle. The tell is the “I helped you in June” conversation in December, which lands as an accusation rather than a claim. Experts therefore spend credit near the time it is earned and do not treat goodwill as a store of value. The corollary is uncomfortable: influence built and then banked for a year is mostly gone.

5. Escalation is an instrument with a computable price

Escalating raises the probability on the current ask and lowers it on future asks with the same counterparty. If escalation moves this ask from 0.30 to 0.90 but reduces the next eight asks from 0.70 to 0.55, the trade costs 1.20 expected asks to buy 0.60 — negative unless this ask is worth more than twice an average one. The tell that someone has misjudged this is a team that cooperates fully on the escalated item and becomes slow on everything else. Experts escalate rarely, jointly, and having told the counterparty first, which halves the future penalty because it removes the betrayal rather than the disagreement.

6. Displacement creates a second, invisible stakeholder

Every yes removes something from a queue, and whoever asked for the displaced item has just lost without being in the room. The tell appears one quarter later as inexplicable friction from a team you never negotiated with. Experts ask the counterparty, at the moment of agreement, what falls out and who asked for it, and then go and tell that person themselves.

7. Silence is the base rate, not a signal

In any matrixed organisation the default answer to a cross-team request is “not this quarter,” delivered by omission because delivering it explicitly invites debate. The observation “nobody objected” is therefore equally likely whether you are winning or losing and carries almost no information. The expert replaces it with a binary that does: is there a named person, a named week, and a line in a document the counterparty wrote?

8. Influence is orthogonal to correctness

The techniques work equally well for wrong decisions, and a practitioner who becomes skilled before becoming calibrated becomes a more efficient source of error. The tell is a track record of winning allocations followed by results that do not show up in any metric. The discipline is to specify, before the campaign, the observation that would make you withdraw the request — and for Arvind, whose direct financial case is thin, that specification is the honest centre of the whole exercise.

9. The forum is chosen before the argument is made

Which meeting a decision is taken in determines the outcome more often than what is said in it, because the forum fixes who is present, what evidence counts and who chairs. The tell is a practitioner who prepares brilliantly for a review owned by the function whose interests the proposal damages. Experts treat forum selection as the first substantive move and will delay a proposal by six weeks to have it heard in the right room.

Section 7Variation by product type and stage

In consumer products the dominant currency is evidence that the counterparty can re-run: an experiment, a cohort chart, a funnel. Consumer organisations are instrumented to settle disputes empirically, and a product manager who brings an argument where a test was possible has forfeited the advantage. In B2B and enterprise, the dominant currency is customer proximity — a named account, a named buyer, a dated renewal risk — because enterprise organisations cannot run experiments at meaningful sample size and substitute account evidence instead. In platforms and marketplaces, as established, currency trade frequently fails because the conflict is structural; the distinguishing expert move is to escalate earlier than feels comfortable to whoever owns both sides.

In hardware and physical goods, the binding constraint is cycle asynchrony, and influence is exercised months before the case exists, on options rather than features. In AI products, the binding constraint is specification: the counterparty cannot commit to an outcome, so the currency is evaluation infrastructure. It is worth saying plainly where the difference is not real: the five-step mechanics — find the allocator, learn the scoreboard, price the ask in their units, reframe or pay, convert to a costly signal — are identical in all five, and claims that any of these domains requires a fundamentally different approach usually turn out to be claims about the counterparty's units, not about the method.

Stage changes texture more than substance. In a company of forty, influence is fast, personal and memory-dominated; currencies are informal, everyone knows what everyone said, and one mishandled escalation is recounted for years. At two thousand people, influence is calendar-dominated: the planning cycle is the only real lever, currencies are formalised into headcount and objectives, and the expected value of a request made three weeks before planning is several times that of the identical request made three weeks after. The single most valuable stage-specific skill in a large company is simply knowing the dates.

Example two: Ojasvin's thin case

Arvind's numbers are less comfortable. Removing 7,200 visits a year at ₹4,800 revenue and ₹3,100 cost destroys ₹1.22 crore of annual service margin. Against that: instrument downtime per calibration event falls from a median 31 hours to about 4; laboratories cite downtime in 22 per cent of non-renewals; the annual non-renewal base is 7.4 per cent of 2,900 instruments, or 215 units at ₹6.2 lakh each, ₹13.3 crore of revenue, of which the downtime-attributable share is ₹2.93 crore. If OTA halves that, the saving is ₹1.47 crore. Add the flash-memory cost of ₹340 per unit on 4,800 units a year, ₹16.3 lakh. Net: ₹1.47 crore − ₹1.22 crore − ₹0.16 crore = ₹9 lakh a year, on assumptions that could each be wrong by a third.

An expert does two things here that a competent practitioner does not. He states the thinness first, in his own voice, before Meenal Deshpande's finance partner finds it — which converts an ambush into a shared problem. And he separates the decision into the part that is cheap and irreversible-if-missed (the flash memory, ₹16.3 lakh a year, decided on 9 February) from the part that is expensive and postponable (the firmware, the submission, the service-model change). The ask on 9 February is not “approve OTA”; it is “buy a ₹16.3 lakh option on OTA,” which is a completely different conversation and one Girish Pai can say yes to without adjudicating a strategy.

Example three: where it failed — Odhani Living

Odhani Living, a Jaipur-based direct-to-consumer home textiles brand, gives the instructive negative. In the June quarter, product manager Tarun Saigal wanted the warehouse operations team to adopt a four-grade returns inspection process replacing a two-grade one; the prize was recovering roughly ₹62 lakh a year of inventory currently written down to zero. Operations declined twice on capacity grounds: the new process added 40 seconds per unit across 18,000 monthly returns, which is 200 hours a month, about 1.4 additional staff. Tarun escalated to the chief operating officer, who directed the change. It was implemented on schedule.

Ninety days later, grading accuracy measured against an audit sample was 61 per cent, against 88 per cent for the old two-grade process. Recovered value was ₹11 lakh annualised, not ₹62 lakh, and the write-down of mis-graded stock exceeded the gain. The failure was not of analysis — the ₹62 lakh was real — but of the difference between compliance and commitment. Operations executed the literal specification with no additional staff, absorbing 200 hours a month by compressing inspection time elsewhere. Nobody sabotaged anything. They did exactly what was directed and nothing that was not.

The recovery took two quarters and is worth reporting precisely, because it is what practitioners rarely see. Tarun stopped defending the process and asked the warehouse supervisor a different question: what would make four-grade inspection faster than two-grade? The answer was a photograph-based reference card at each station, which the supervisor had suggested a year earlier to someone else and which cost ₹40,000. Accuracy reached 84 per cent within a quarter. The lesson Tarun drew — that the escalation had bought him the allocation and cost him the expertise — is the most expensive form of this subject's central point, and the cheapest diagnostic that would have caught it was available on day one: ask the counterparty how they would do it, and notice whether the answer is a plan or a shrug.
