Section 10Where experts genuinely disagree

Three disputes are live, and a practitioner who pretends they are settled will give bad advice.

Whether influence should be necessary at all. The evidentialist position, held seriously inside several large technology firms, is that a well-designed organisation makes lateral persuasion unnecessary: if the decision turns on a number, instrument the number and let the allocation follow. Its strongest form is not naive — it concedes that measurement is incomplete and argues that every hour spent on persuasion is an hour not spent fixing the measurement, and that organisations which valorise influence systematically under-invest in instrumentation and reward articulate people over correct ones. The evidence it rests on is the observable superiority of experiment-driven allocation in consumer software. It would be wrong if a material share of important decisions turn on quantities that cannot be measured in time to matter — which is exactly Arvind's situation, where the value of OTA is an option on unknown future firmware fixes.

Whether reciprocity is the mechanism or a description. The exchange school treats currencies as causal: find the right one and the allocation follows. The structural school's steelman is that apparent currency trades are epiphenomena — what actually determined the outcome was who controlled the forum, the metric and the budget, and the favour merely provided a face-saving account. Its evidence is the consistency with which the same individual, transferred between organisations, becomes influential or not depending on reporting structure rather than technique. It would be wrong if practitioners in identical structural positions showed large and stable differences in outcomes, which is precisely what the exchange school believes the data show and neither side has established cleanly.

Whether influence is a virtue or a symptom. A minority but serious position holds that the celebration of “influence without authority” in product management is a rationalisation of a design defect: a role given full accountability and no control, where the skill required is real but its necessity is a management failure that the literature helps organisations avoid confronting. The steelman is Kanter's: responsibility without power reliably produces defensive behaviour, and the population of product managers who burn out is not evidence of individual inadequacy. It would be wrong if organisations that granted product managers direct authority over engineering resources produced better outcomes — and the mixed record of that arrangement, which tends to produce faster decisions of lower quality, is the strongest available argument against it.

Section 11What mastery looks like

Someone who has internalised this behaves differently in four observable ways. They begin with the counterparty's arithmetic rather than their own, and can state, unprompted, what each key stakeholder reports upward and when. They design the sequence and the forum before writing the argument, and will accept a six-week delay to be heard in the right room. They ask for something small and dated at the end of every conversation, and treat the absence of a costly signal as a refusal rather than as progress. And they hold their own proposals to the standard they ask others to accept, which shows up most clearly in their willingness to say, as Arvind must, that a case is thin.

The negative test is equally diagnostic. Someone who has merely studied the subject talks about stakeholders in the language of personality, prepares the deck before choosing the meeting, reports “alignment” as an outcome, and is surprised in November by a decision that was made in September.

Section 12Decisions, and questions for discussion

Nandita withdraws the deactivation proposal on 16 February and substitutes two things. The first is a 90-day pilot in two categories — ethnic womenswear and home furnishing — which requires four approvals rather than six and no change to Harsh's target, because pilot deactivations are excluded from the count. The second, which she treats as the actual campaign, is a written proposal to the chief operating officer to redefine net new active sellers as sellers active and SLA-compliant at day 60. She has concluded that she is not in an influence contest with Harsh Vora but in a measurement dispute with the company, and that the pilot exists primarily to produce the evidence that makes the measurement argument unanswerable in the next planning cycle.

Arvind does not ask for OTA on 9 February. He asks Girish Pai for the flash-memory provision alone, priced at ₹16.3 lakh a year, presented explicitly as an option rather than a commitment, with a written note that the product case is currently worth about ₹9 lakh a year and is not yet strong enough to justify the firmware and regulatory work. He tells Meenal Deshpande before he tells anyone else, and asks her a question rather than presenting a conclusion: what would the service organisation need to be measured on for a reduction in visits to be good news? That question, not the flash memory, is the one that determines whether OTA ever ships.
